California governor vetoes butane hash oil law

View image | gettyimages.com California governor critical of hard-on-crime legislation and overcrowded prisons

Governor Jerry Brown vetoed a law that would have created new penalties for incurring injuries on others while extracting cannabis with flammable chemicals.

Brown said California already has enough criminal laws and advised holding off on any new criminal laws that would contribute to an already terrible prison overcrowding situation in the state, as reported by East Bay Express.

Explosions and fires caused by butane hash oil manufacturing are a growing problem in California.

Nearly 10 percent of severe burn cases at Northern California’s UC Davis Medical Center and Shriners Hospitals for Children are now attributed to butane hash oil (BHO) explosions, as reported by The Sacramento Bee. That’s more burn victims from BHO explosions than from car wrecks and house fires combined.

Although arson, criminal negligence and BHO production are all crimes in California already, lawmakers wanted to create a separate crime for BHO makers who injure others.

More from East Bay Express:

After a BHO fire in Walnut Creek, Assembly Bill 849 . . . wanted to send a message to hash blasters by creating a new crime carrying prison sentences of up to six years for BHO-makers who hurt others. The bill passed the Assembly unanimously on August 31.

The Governor sent a message to members of the California State Assembly, explaining his decision to veto the hash oil bill along with eight other bills:

“Each of these bills creates a new crime ? usually by finding a novel way to characterize and criminalize conduct that is already proscribed. This multiplication and particularization of criminal behavior creates increasing complexity without commensurate benefit.

Over the last several decades, California’s criminal code has grown to more than 5,000 separate provisions, covering almost every conceivable form of human misbehavior. During the same period, our jail and prison populations have exploded.

Before we keep going down this road, I think we should pause and reflect on how our system of criminal justice could be made more human, more just and more cost-effective.”
